ideas.hypothesis: Firms whose pre-2008 balance sheets had smaller currency, maturity and leverage mismatches (the vulnerabilities targeted by the IMF Balance Sheet Approach to crisis prevention) suffered smaller and shorter ROE declines in the post-crisis period, and these balance-sheet indicators predict post-crisis recovery better than ownership type such as Bumiputera control.

sources.role: mechanism: sectoral balance-sheet composition (size and composition of assets and liabilities) as the source of crisis vulnerability and the target of prevention
method and measure: ROE as performance measure and Wilcoxon signed-rank comparisons of crisis vs post-crisis periods for Malaysian listed firms
setting: post-2008 call to redesign financial governance around crisis prevention
mechanism: critique that standard macro models ignored balance-sheet frictions relevant to crisis prevention
finding: access to financial resources, rather than group identity, drives vulnerability, motivating balance-sheet rather than identity-based predictors

ideas.test: Panel of roughly 300 Bursa Malaysia listed firms (including Bumiputera-controlled firms) for 2005-2013 from annual reports or a commercial database. Compute 2006-2007 leverage, short-term debt share and foreign-currency debt share; measure the change in ROE between crisis (2008-2009) and post-crisis (2010-2013) years. Run Wilcoxon signed-rank tests within mismatch terciles and a regression of the ROE change and years-to-recovery on the mismatch indicators, a Bumiputera-control dummy, industry and size controls.
ideas.disconfirming: Pre-crisis mismatch indicators have no significant association with the depth or duration of the post-crisis ROE decline, or ownership type explains the post-crisis trajectory while balance-sheet indicators add nothing.

ideas.hypothesis: State consumer-protection bans on for-profit foreclosure rescue operations (such as Massachusetts in 2007) reduced equity-stripping sale-leaseback transfers and completed foreclosures among distressed owners, thereby shrinking the negative price externality that foreclosures impose on neighboring homes.

sources.role: setting and mechanism: Massachusetts permanent ban on for-profit foreclosure rescue and the equity-stripping mechanism
method and measure: hedonic price regression valuing external effects of nearby foreclosures
setting: Dodd-Frank consumer-protection provisions as the federal analogue of state-level prevention policy
mechanism: realignment of financial governance toward prevention after the 2008 crisis

ideas.test: Difference-in-differences using county deed and foreclosure records for 2005-2010 in Massachusetts versus neighboring states without bans (e.g., Connecticut, New Hampshire, Rhode Island). Outcomes: count of non-arms-length sale-leaseback transfers, foreclosure completion rate among properties with a notice of default, and the hedonic sale-price discount for homes within 0.1 and 0.25 miles of a foreclosure. Compare pre- and post-September 2007 changes.
ideas.disconfirming: No relative decline in rescue-type transfers or foreclosure completions in Massachusetts after the ban, or an unchanged or larger neighbor price discount relative to control states.

ideas.hypothesis: Consistent with Minsky's financial instability hypothesis, the relationship between neighborhood household debt burden and foreclosure incidence is nonlinear with a critical threshold, and that threshold is lower in neighborhoods saturated with high-cost (predatory) mortgage lending.

sources.role: mechanism and method: nonlinear threshold in the debt ratio beyond which debt turns from stimulus to financial stress
mechanism: Minsky's hedge-speculative-Ponzi financing framework applied to the US mortgage collapse
setting: spatially and racially concentrated high-cost lending in inner-city and Sun Belt neighborhoods
mechanism: delinquency triggers cascades of trouble that make highly indebted households fragile
setting: predatory practices surrounding distressed homeowners in the 2007-08 foreclosure crisis

ideas.test: Census-tract panel for 5-10 metropolitan areas, 2004-2010: HMDA data for high-cost loan share and loan-to-income ratios, plus tract foreclosure filing rates from county records or RealtyTrac-type data. Estimate a Hansen threshold regression of the foreclosure rate on average loan-to-income, allowing the threshold to differ between tracts above and below the median high-cost loan share; control for unemployment and house price change.
ideas.disconfirming: A linear model fits as well as the threshold model (no significant threshold), or the estimated threshold does not differ between high- and low-high-cost-lending tracts.
